hints: Look closely at the carbon that carries the chlorine in 1-chloro-2-methylbutane, is it primary, secondary or tertiary?
Remember that a primary halogenoalkane with a strong nucleophile like cyanide strongly favours SN2, which goes through a single transition state with no carbocation.
Picture the SN2 transition state with both the incoming group and the leaving group partly bonded to the same carbon, then check which diagram keeps the correct two H atoms on that carbon.
walkthrough:
**Draw out the starting halogenoalkane**

Great start, let's see what we are working with. 1-chloro-2-methylbutane is $\text{ClCH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

The C bonded to Cl is bonded to only one other carbon, so it is a primary halogenoalkane: $\text{-CH}_2\text{Cl}$.

**Decide SN1 or SN2**

Now think mechanism. Cyanide, $\text{CN}^-$, is a strong nucleophile.

Primary halogenoalkanes undergo SN2 because a primary carbocation, $\text{+CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, would be very unstable. So we expect one concerted step with a transition state, not a carbocation intermediate:
$$\text{NC}^- + \text{R-CH}_2\text{-Cl} \rightarrow [\text{NC} \cdots \text{CH}_2 \cdots \text{Cl}]^- \rightarrow \text{R-CH}_2\text{-CN} + \text{Cl}^-$$

**Match the correct transition state**

In the SN2 transition state the central carbon is temporarily 5-coordinate, with partial bonds shown as dashed lines: $\text{NC} \cdots \text{C} \cdots \text{Cl}$.

That carbon must still carry its original three groups, which are two H atoms and one $\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ group. This matches exactly the negatively charged species with two H atoms on top.

options.A: This is the SN2 transition state for the correct molecule. The central carbon has the two H atoms and the $\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ group it starts with, plus partial bonds to both $\text{NC}$ and $\text{Cl}$ with an overall negative charge. This is exactly expected for a primary chloroalkane with $\text{CN}^-$.
options.B: This is an SN2 transition state but for the wrong isomer. It shows a carbon bonded to $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, which would come from 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, a tertiary halogenoalkane, not 1-chloro-2-methylbutane.
options.C: This is a tertiary carbocation, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. It is the SN1 intermediate for 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, not for our primary starting material. Students choosing this have mixed up the position of the Cl.
options.D: This is the primary carbocation $\text{+CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Although it has the right carbon skeleton, a primary carbocation is far too unstable to form readily, so SN1 is very unlikely here. The reaction will go by SN2 instead.
